newsitem.title: UK: Dlr jumps hurdles in Europe in race to 1.51 marks.
newsitem.headline: Dlr jumps hurdles in Europe in race to 1.51 marks.

text.p: A wave of fund buying triggered stop-loss dollar buying near 1.5050/60 marks in the European afternoon, and overall mark weakness and Swiss franc losses propelled it within a fraction of the 1.51 psychological goal.

A break of 1.5050/60 marks and 1.2300 Swiss francs were technical catalysts as both were key 50 retracements of the dollar's May to July decline. Jangling nerves over a near-term rise in U.S. rates added fundamental support, analysts said.
The dollar rose to 1.5090 before before profit-taking pushed it to 1.5079/86 marks by 1443 GMT versus Monday's 1.4910/13.

Jiro Nagato, senior dealer at Sumitomo Bank in London, said the dollar's move in Europe was ignited in dollar/Swiss after the Swiss National Bank was seen injecting ample liquidity into the money market this morning.
Although current Swiss franc weakness is attributed more to dollar strength, economists said the Swiss unit was long overdue for a period of independent weakness given its weak economy.

The high-yielding lira continued to benefit from overall mark lethargy as talk of the lira's return to the ERM at 1,000 bubbled. It rose to 1006.05/55 per mark at 1517 GMT versus 1011.00/35 late on Monday.
Focus is on the Fed and a possible credit-tightening as the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting approaches on September 24.
Speculation is intensifying ahead of the Beige Book tomorrow and producer and consumer prices on Thursday and Friday respectively. Retail sales data are also due on Friday.

Lehman's Holm also said there was a possibility that the Fed may raise the federal funds target rate by 25 basis points from the current 5.25 percent soon because raising interest rates a day before the U.S. presidential debate begins on September 25 was likely to ruffle political feathers.
Despite the anxiety over a possible U.S. rate rise, some analysts and dealers said a tightening has already been factored in and that the dollar was looking overbought at current levels.

David Brown, economist at Bear Stearns in London, said the dollar was still subject to some short-term corrective losses. He noted that during the course of 1994, when the federal funds rate was doubled from 2.5 percent to 5.0 percent, dollar/mark crashed from 1.75 in February 1994 to 1.35 a year later.
In other dollar pairs, the dollar surpassed 109.45 yen resistance and was within grasp of the 110 target by 1542 GMT versus Monday's 109.03/10. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 6721
